schopenhauer|The whole foundation on which our existence rests is the present—the ever-fleeting present. It lies, then, in the very nature of our existence to take the form of constant motion, and to offer no possibility of our ever attaining the rest for which we are always striving. We are like a man running downhill, who cannot keep on his legs unless he runs on, and will inevitably fall if he stops; or, again, like a pole balanced on the tip of one's finger; or like a planet, which would fall into its sun the moment it ceased to hurry forward on its way. Unrest is the mark of existence.|Arthur Schopenhauer, Studies in Pessimism (tr. T. Bailey Saunders)|meaning,time,truth

schopenhauer|Life presents itself chiefly as a task—the task, I mean, of subsisting at all, gagner sa vie. If this is accomplished, life is a burden, and then there comes the second task of doing something with that which has been won—of warding off boredom, which, like a bird of prey, hovers over us, ready to fall wherever it sees a life secure from need. The first task is to win something; the second, to banish the feeling that it has been won; otherwise it is a burden.|Arthur Schopenhauer, Studies in Pessimism (tr. T. Bailey Saunders)|work
schopenhauer|Human life must be some kind of mistake. The truth of this will be sufficiently obvious if we only remember that man is a compound of needs and necessities hard to satisfy; and that even when they are satisfied, all he obtains is a state of painlessness, where nothing remains to him but abandonment to boredom. This is direct proof that existence has no real value in itself; for what is boredom but the feeling of the emptiness of life? If life—the craving for which is the very essence of our being—were possessed of any positive intrinsic value, there would be no such thing as boredom at all: mere existence would satisfy us in itself, and we should want for nothing.|Arthur Schopenhauer, Studies in Pessimism (tr. petrarch|Yon nightingale, whose bursts of thrilling tone,\nPour'd in soft sorrow from her tuneful throat,\nHaply her mate or infant brood bemoan,\nFilling the fields and skies with pity's note;\nHere lingering till the long long night is gone,\nAwakes the memory of my cruel lot—\nBut I my wretched self must wail alone:\nFool, who secure from death an angel thought!\nO easy duped, who thus on hope relies!\nWho would have deem'd the darkness, which appears,\nFrom orbs more brilliant than the sun should rise?\nNow know I, made by sad experience wise,\nThat Fate would teach me by a life of tears,\nOn wings how fleeting fast all earthly rapture flies!|Petrarch, Canzoniere (tr. petrarch|Warfare I cannot wage, yet know not peace;\nI fear, I hope, I burn, I freeze again;\nMount to the skies, then bow to earth my face;\nGrasp the whole world, yet nothing can obtain.\nHis prisoner Love nor frees, nor will detain;\nIn toils he holds me not, nor will release;\nHe slays me not, nor yet will he unchain;\nNor joy allows, nor lets my sorrow cease.\nSightless I see my fair; though mute, I mourn;\nI scorn existence, and yet court its stay;\nDetest myself, and for another burn;\nBy grief I'm nurtured; and, though tearful, gay;\nDeath I despise, and life alike I hate:\nSuch, lady, dost thou make my wayward state!|Petrarch, Canzoniere (tr. michelangelo|When divine Art conceives a form and face,\nShe bids the craftsman for his first essay\nTo shape a simple model in mere clay:\nThis is the earliest birth of Art's embrace.\nFrom the live marble in the second place\nHis mallet brings into the light of day\nA thing so beautiful that who can say\nWhen time shall conquer that immortal grace?\nThus my own model I was born to be—\nThe model of that nobler self, whereto\nSchooled by your pity, lady, I shall grow.\nEach overplus and each deficiency\nYou will make good. michelangelo|How can that be, lady, which all men learn\nBy long experience? Shapes that seem alive,\nWrought in hard mountain marble, will survive\nTheir maker, whom the years to dust return!\nThus to effect cause yields. Art hath her turn,\nAnd triumphs over Nature. I, who strive\nWith Sculpture, know this well; her wonders live\nIn spite of time and death, those tyrants stern.\nSo I can give long life to both of us\nIn either way, by colour or by stone,\nMaking the semblance of thy face and mine.\nCenturies hence when both are buried, thus\nThy beauty and my sadness shall be shown,\nAnd men shall say, 'For her 'twas wise to pine.'|Michelangelo, Sonnets (tr.
